2232-the-duchess-of-malfi:
John Webster's Jacobean tragedy centers on a widowed duchess who secretly marries her steward, defying her powerful brothers. The Duchess of Malfi moves from court intrigue to murder and madness as the brothers' spies close in, and the duchess faces her fate with famous courage. Webster's verse is dark, poetic, and full of skulls, shadows, and whispered plots.

The play is bloody even by its age's standards, yet its heroine's dignity gives it lasting force. Themes of power, gender, and corrupt authority run beneath the horror. For readers of early drama, it stands as one of the great tragedies of the English stage.
4788-mademoiselle-fifi:
Guy de Maupassant's Mademoiselle Fifi gathers a preface, the title story, and Boule de Suif. Its preface traces Maupassant's life, beginning at the Chateau de Miromesnil near Dieppe, where he was born on August 5, 1850. The Maupassants were an old Lorraine family settled in Normandy in the middle of the eighteenth century, and his father married Laure Le Poittevin in 1846.

With her brother Alfred, Laure had been playmate of Gustave Flaubert, son of a Rouen surgeon, who would direct her son's literary life. A woman of no common literary accomplishments, fond of the classics and especially Shakespeare, she separated from her husband and kept her two sons, Guy and his younger brother Hervé. Until thirteen, Guy lived with his mother at Etretat, between sea and luxuriant country, growing fond of nature and outdoor sports and fishing with fishermen. Readers get two famous Maupassant stories, framed by his boyhood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amalfi:
Amalfi's archdiocese, directly dependent on the Holy See, sits at Amalfi near Naples, populous between the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. A free republic from the seventh century to 1075, it matched Pisa and Genoa in prosperity and sea power. It then fell prey to the Normans as one of their chief posts. Emperor Lothair fought there for Innocent II against Sicily's King Roger, who backed Antipope Anacletus.

In medieval culture Amalfi held a worthy place through flourishing schools of law and mathematics. Its republican prosperity, Norman capture, and imperial wars trace a small city's large place in southern Italy's story.

mademoiselle-fifi:
Mademoiselle Fifi is a book of stories by Guy de Maupassant. A preface here tells his life, from his birth in 1850 near Dieppe. His mother, Laure, had played with Gustave Flaubert as a girl. Flaubert later guided her son's first steps in writing.

Young Guy grew up at Etretat, between sea and green country. The title tale is set in the Franco-Prussian War. A slight, fair Prussian officer is nicknamed Mademoiselle Fifi by his comrades. 'Boule de Suif,' his most famous story, stands beside it. Maupassant's tales are clear, cold, and perfectly made. Few writers have matched his art of the short story.
nasa-tm-19650012596-an-evaluation-of-the:
W E Daniels, Shirley J Hendricks, and Duane C Jensen at Goddard produced this December 1964 evaluation of Earth's main magnetic field. It covers the years 1940 to 1962. Their work rests on magnetic survey data and on yearly mean values from observatories around the world.

A good field model matters for navigation, for spacecraft work, and for science. Earth's field changes slowly over time, so old data must be combined with care. The authors build a new determination of the field from that long record. Readers get both the result and the data base behind it, spanning more than two decades.
nasa-tm-19680016262-determination-of-the:
Reuven Ramaty of Goddard Space Flight Center and Richard E. Lingenfelter of the University of California at Los Angeles wrote this May 1968 preprint, X-611-68-208. Their topic is a Type IV solar radio burst, a strong radio outburst from high in the Sun's outer air, called the corona. From that one signal they seek the corona's magnetic field and the energy of its radio-emitting electrons.

The pair calculate how fast electrons spiraling in a magnetic field give off radio waves, called gyro-synchrotron emission. They show the burst's sharp low and high frequency cutoffs fit that process in ionized gas. Given the gas density near the burst, the observed spectrum then yields both the field strength and the electron energy range.
nasa-tm-19680017934-an-experimental-stud:
Roy L. Marshall, Gerald L. Pellett, and Andrew R. Saunders of Langley Research Center measured the drag of burning aluminum droplets in this study, presented in October 1966. Burning particles move through many combustion systems, so their motion matters. The team watched droplets between about 200 and 500 microns wide as they burned.

The droplets fell through still ambient air while burning. The team tracked their motion to find the effective drag force on each one. Their starting idea was that a burning droplet feels quite different drag than a cold one. The results feed models of multi-phase combustion flows. Such models guide the design of burners and rocket systems using metal fuels.
nasa-tm-19700008713-current-density-mapp:
Robert M. Masters and Francis J. Stenger of the Lewis Research Center studied cadmium sulfide thin-film solar cells. Such cells can lose power where the current flows unevenly. Their report presents a fast way to find those weak spots.

The method measures the magnetic field just above the face of the cell. From those readings it draws a map of where the current runs strong or weak. The map is shown in graphic form, so uneven regions can be seen at a glance. A quick check of this kind helps makers spot flawed cells early.
nasa-tm-19710007024-evaluation-of-linear:
Richard J. Mittendorf of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in February 1971. It evaluates two plastics for use as irradiation capsules. Sealed capsules hold experiments while they are exposed to radiation in a reactor.

Both capsule types were irradiated inside metal containers at the Plum Brook Reactor. The goal was to fix the safe working limits for each plastic. Limits for the polyethylene capsules were defined by the tests, Mittendorf reports. The epoxy capsules turned highly radioactive under exposure. They also failed at lower exposure levels than the polyethylene ones.

podcast-tuckercarlson-5x9vR5sKHFI:
Tucker Carlson devotes this episode to what he calls the secret history of the Bible's strangest figures. They are the giants and demons of scripture. He also covers the advanced civilizations he says flourished before the Great Flood destroyed them. The discussion treats the early chapters of Genesis as a suppressed record rather than myth.

Carlson and his material move between the biblical text, ancient sources, and modern alternative archaeology. The flood story appears in many cultures, and the episode leans on that spread as evidence of a real, shared memory. Mainstream scholars read these texts differently, and listeners should know the claims are contested. Preserved here is a popular broadcaster's full argument that the ancient world was stranger, and better informed, than the modern one admits.
the-chronology-of-ancient-kingdoms-amend:
Sir Isaac Newton wrote this work on ancient dates, printed in London in 1728 for J. Tonson, J. Osborn, and T. Longman. Its title promises an amended chronology of ancient kingdoms, with a short chronicle prefixed. That chronicle runs from the first memory of things in Europe to Alexander the Great's conquest of Persia.

A dedication to the Queen presents the book as Newton's last work. The writer of that address calls it an offering from as great a genius as any age has produced. He notes the Queen's steady support for arts and sciences, and the many honors she had shown the author. On those grounds, he argues, this work above the rest claims her protection. Readers get Newton's late attempt to rebuild the timeline of the ancient world on stricter evidence, compressing reigns that older histories had stretched far too long.
the-duchess-of-malfi:
John Webster's tragedy The Duchess of Malfi comes with a front note on the playwright's dim life. His birth and death dates are mere guesses, the note says; he first shows up in 1602 writing plays with others for Henslowe. Four plays are his alone, and this one was printed in 1623, though it may have been writ as early as 1611.

Drawn from Bandello through Painter, the plot shows a widowed duchess who weds her steward in secret. Her brothers' rage brings spies, madness, and death. Webster's dark verse still chills the stage.
